sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Defines the base course as the layer immediately below the pavement surface, and defines subbase as the layer or layers located below the base and above the subgrade, establishing the vertical layer terminology used throughout the chapter.
sections.body: The layer immediately below the pavement surface is the base course. The term subbase designates the layer(s) below the base and above the subgrade.
key_points: Base course: the layer immediately below the pavement surface.
Subbase: the layer(s) located below the base course and above the subgrade.
sections.applicability: Applies as the terminology reference for all base and subbase discussion in this chapter.

sections.title: Subgrade Protection
sections.summary: Warns that granular subbase and base layers left exposed over a winter in a wet-freeze region can soften the subgrade beneath them, recommends covering these layers with the pavement, and cautions that construction traffic can destabilize an exposed subgrade when resuming work.
sections.body: Subbase and base course granular layers left exposed over a winter in a wet-freeze region can cause softening of the subgrade. These layers should be covered with the pavement; if this is not possible, use caution when resuming construction, since construction traffic can make a subgrade unstable.
key_points: Granular subbase/base layers left exposed through a winter in a wet-freeze region can soften the underlying subgrade.
Cover subbase/base layers with the pavement whenever possible to prevent this softening.
If layers must remain exposed, use caution resuming construction because traffic can destabilize the subgrade.
sections.applicability: Applies to projects in wet-freeze climates where subbase or base layers may be left exposed over winter before paving.

sections.title: Subbase Course
sections.summary: Describes subbase as natural or crushed granular material with CBR values of 20 to 100, used for frost protection or subgrade drainage, with a 3 percent fines limit in frost areas, and details placement practices covering equipment, moisture-density control, layer thickness, subgrade evaluation, traffic management, density verification, grade tolerance, surface protection, and rolling equipment.
sections.body: Subbase materials are generally granular materials, either natural or crushed, with CBR values that range from 20 to 100. These materials are generally used as subgrade protection layers (frost protection) or to provide drainage above the subgrade. In frost areas, the percent of material passing the No. 200 sieve (0.075 mm) is limited to 3 percent. Important elements for subbase placement include: starting placement along the centerline or high point to maintain drainage during construction; performing placement using automated equipment or a stone box on a bulldozer; developing moisture-density relationships in the laboratory using the modified Proctor test (ASTM D1557/CRD-C 162) for aircraft/vehicle traffic greater than 27,215 kg (60,000 lb), or the standard Proctor test (ASTM D698/CRD-C 653) for lighter traffic, keeping material within 1 percent of optimum moisture as best practice (free-draining subbase materials may use a lower moisture content to avoid adding excess water to the subgrade during compaction); using a layer thickness three to four times the largest aggregate size, since a thickness close to the largest aggregate size adversely affects density, grading, and smoothness; evaluating the subgrade for stability and repairing soft areas prior to subbase placement; implementing traffic management in front of placement to eliminate potential problems; permitting nuclear gauges to monitor subbase density; verifying density with one-point tests at the delivered moisture content, performed twice a day; holding the subbase grade tolerance to 13 mm (0.5 in.) using a 4.8 m (16 ft) straightedge, with laser auto-graders or auto-trimmers recommended on larger projects and relaxed tolerances considered where automated equipment cannot be justified; protecting the surface once placed by providing drainage so water does not pond and watering if dry conditions prevail; and rolling with vibratory drum rollers, switching to rubber tire rollers if compaction is difficult since the kneading action of the wheels aids compaction.
key_points: Subbase is granular (natural or crushed) with CBR 20 to 100, used for frost protection or drainage above the subgrade.
In frost areas, limit fines passing the No. 200 sieve (0.075 mm) to 3 percent.
Use modified Proctor (ASTM D1557/CRD-C 162) for traffic > 27,215 kg (60,000 lb), standard Proctor (ASTM D698/CRD-C 653) for lighter traffic; keep moisture within about 1% of optimum.
Layer thickness must be 3 to 4 times the largest aggregate size to avoid density, grading, and smoothness problems.
Grade tolerance for subbase: 13 mm (0.5 in.) using a 4.8 m (16 ft) straightedge; laser auto-graders/trimmers recommended on larger projects.
Verify density with one-point tests at delivered moisture content, performed twice a day; nuclear gauges are permitted.
Evaluate and repair soft subgrade areas before placement, and manage construction traffic ahead of placement.
Roll with vibratory drum rollers; use rubber tire rollers if compaction proves difficult (kneading action aids compaction).
sections.applicability: Applies to the placement, moisture/density control, and quality control of granular subbase courses beneath concrete pavement.

sections.title: Base Course
sections.summary: Describes base course as similar to subbase material but of higher quality, notes that rigid pavement base requirements are less restrictive than for flexible pavements, references UFC 3-260-02 for proof rolling, and lists placement precautions including checking the underlying course, avoiding wet/frozen conditions, roller selection, and grade tolerance.
sections.body: A good base course is important to avoid or minimize construction difficulties. Base course materials are similar to subbase materials but are usually of higher quality in terms of crushed aggregate content, deleterious material, and gradation. The requirements for bases under rigid concrete pavement are less restrictive than for flexible pavements; therefore, the designer must select the correct requirements and guide specifications for concrete pavements. Requirements for proof rolling of the completed base course are given in UFC 3-260-02. The critical elements for base course placement are the same as those described for subbase materials, with the following additions: check the underlying course (subgrade or subbase) before placing and spreading the base course, correcting and compacting any ruts or soft/yielding areas (from improper drainage, hauling, or other causes) to the required density before placing the base; do not place the base if the underlying course is wet, muddy, or frozen; suspend work on the base course during freezing temperatures or if the base material contains frozen material; use vibratory rollers, rubber tire rollers, and static wheel rollers for compaction, with some materials allowing the vibratory roller alone to achieve compaction and a smooth, even surface; and hold the grade tolerance for base layers to 10 mm (3/8 in.) across a 4.8 m (16 ft) distance, which usually requires automated placement methods to attain the tight tolerance.
key_points: Base course is similar to subbase but of higher quality: more crushed aggregate content, less deleterious material, tighter gradation.
Rigid pavement base requirements are less restrictive than for flexible pavements; the designer must select the correct guide specification.
Proof rolling requirements for the completed base course are given in UFC 3-260-02.
Check and correct/compact the underlying course (ruts, soft/yielding areas) to required density before placing the base.
Do not place base on a wet, muddy, or frozen underlying course; suspend base work during freezing or if the material is frozen.
Compact with vibratory, rubber tire, and static wheel rollers; some materials can be handled with the vibratory roller alone.
Grade tolerance for base layers: 10 mm (3/8 in.) over a 4.8 m (16 ft) distance, usually requiring automated placement methods.
sections.applicability: Applies to the placement and quality control of the base course layer directly beneath rigid concrete pavement.

sections.title: Chemically Stabilized Base Courses
sections.summary: Explains that DoD does not mandate stabilized bases under concrete pavement (decided project-by-project), that cement is the most common stabilizer, and that stabilized-layer strength/stiffness increases with cement content, affecting curling/warping restraint and cracking risk while improving fatigue life and constructability when well designed.
sections.body: DoD does not require stabilized base courses under concrete pavements; the need for stabilization is determined on a project-by-project basis. There are several types of stabilized bases; cement stabilization is the most commonly used stabilizer, although asphalt cement, lime, or other materials are also used. The properties and qualities of a cement-stabilized material depend upon the amount of cement added -- strength and stiffness of the stabilized layer increase with increasing cement content. The stiffness of stabilized base layers affects the performance of concrete pavements: it influences the curling/warping behavior of a slab and increases the restraint on the slab during the initial curing period. With higher amounts of cement, the stiffness of a lean concrete base can become extremely high, increasing the potential for random cracking, reflective cracking, or cracking due to unsupported slab edges. However, a well-designed and well-constructed stabilized base increases the fatigue life and improves the constructability of a concrete pavement. Details are available in UFC 3-250-11.
key_points: DoD does not require a stabilized base under concrete pavement; the decision is made project-by-project.
Cement is the most common stabilizer; asphalt cement, lime, and other materials are also used.
Stabilized-layer strength and stiffness increase with the amount of cement added.
Higher stiffness affects slab curling/warping and increases initial-cure restraint, raising cracking risk (random, reflective, or unsupported-edge cracking) at high cement contents.
A well-designed, well-constructed stabilized base increases fatigue life and improves constructability.
UFC 3-250-11, Soil Stabilization and Modification for Pavements, provides stabilized-base design/construction details.
sections.applicability: Applies when a project team is deciding whether and how to use a chemically stabilized base course beneath rigid concrete pavement.

sections.title: Material Cautions
sections.summary: Flags that lean, porous cement-treated base (CTB) is more susceptible to sulfate attack than pavement concrete, and requires investigating sulfates in soil, groundwater, or aggregates, covering CTB before winter/freezing unless it has attained design strength, and checking grade before resuming spring construction.
sections.body: Lean porous concretes such as cement treated base (CTB) courses are more susceptible to sulfate attack than pavement concretes. During the design phase, possible detrimental effects on the CTB caused by sulfates present in the soil, groundwater, or aggregates should be investigated. A CTB layer should be covered with the pavement layer before winter or a freezing event; if a CTB layer must remain exposed, it must first attain its design strength. Before construction resumes in the spring, the grade should be checked.
key_points: Lean, porous CTB is more susceptible to sulfate attack than pavement concrete; investigate soil/groundwater/aggregate sulfates during design.
Cover CTB with the pavement layer before winter or a freezing event.
If CTB must remain exposed over winter, it must first attain its design strength.
Check the grade before resuming construction in the spring.
sections.applicability: Applies to cement treated base (CTB) and similar lean stabilized base materials, particularly regarding sulfate exposure and winter protection.

sections.title: Strength
sections.summary: Sets the strength thresholds that distinguish a lean concrete material from a stabilized material (compressive strength above 10 MPa/1500 psi, flexural strength above 2.5 MPa/350 psi, or fines passing the No. 200 sieve at 15 percent or less), and requires restricting traffic on lean concrete until it reaches 2,400 kPa (350 psi) compressive strength.
sections.body: The primary issue with lean concrete is the strength of the mixture. If the compressive strength is greater than 10 MPa (1,500 psi), the flexural strength is greater than 2.5 MPa (350 psi), or the amount of material passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve is 15 percent or less, the material is classified as a lean concrete rather than a stabilized material. Traffic on lean concrete must be restricted until it attains a compressive strength of 2,400 kPa (350 psi).
key_points: Material is classified as lean concrete (not stabilized material) if compressive strength > 10 MPa (1,500 psi).
Also classified as lean concrete if flexural strength > 2.5 MPa (350 psi).
Also classified as lean concrete if material passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve is 15% or less.
Restrict traffic on lean concrete until it attains a compressive strength of 2,400 kPa (350 psi).
sections.applicability: Applies when classifying a cement-treated material as lean concrete versus stabilized material, and when deciding when to allow traffic on it.

sections.title: Reflective Cracking
sections.summary: Notes that higher maximum compressive strength in lean concrete increases cracking and reflective-cracking potential, and describes two mitigation methods: aligning the lean concrete's joint pattern with the pavement's joint pattern, and applying a double coat of wax-based curing compound to reduce bonding between the lean concrete and the pavement.
sections.body: As the maximum compressive strength achieved in the lean concrete increases, the potential for cracking, and therefore reflective cracking, increases. One method to counteract cracking is to design joints in the layer; the jointing pattern in the lean concrete must match the joint pattern of the pavement, or reflective cracking may occur, so care must be taken to align the joints when placing the concrete pavement. Another method of preventing reflective cracking is applying a double application of wax-based curing compound to the surface of the lean concrete, which reduces the potential for bonding between the lean concrete and the pavement and minimizes the potential for random cracking in the pavement.
key_points: Higher maximum compressive strength in lean concrete increases the potential for cracking, including reflective cracking.
Mitigation 1: design joints in the lean concrete layer that match the pavement's joint pattern; align joints carefully during pavement placement.
Mitigation 2: apply a double application of wax-based curing compound to the lean concrete surface to reduce bonding with the pavement.
Reducing lean-concrete/pavement bonding minimizes the potential for random cracking in the pavement.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing joint layout and curing procedures for concrete pavement placed over a lean concrete or cement-stabilized base.

sections.title: Drainage Layers
sections.summary: Covers the default inclusion of a drainage layer beneath rigid pavement, the material options (open-graded stabilized/unstabilized, choke-stone-topped, or rapid-draining), the stability-versus-porosity design balance, restrictions on unstabilized open-graded layers under wide-body aircraft loading, and the typical layer thickness of 100 to 150 mm (4 to 6 in.).
sections.body: By default, rigid pavement designs incorporate a drainage layer unless the existing subgrade is highly permeable; normally, the concrete pavement is placed directly on the drainage layer. Drainage layers may be open-graded materials, either unstabilized or stabilized, with subgrade or asphalt cement, open-graded with a finer choke stone surface, or a rapid-draining material that limits fines but includes some sand-sized fraction for better stability under traffic. Construction on unstabilized open-graded materials may require special equipment and operations, so requirements for drainage layers must be clearly stated in the project plans and specifications so the contractor can prepare a realistic bid. Common practice is to use cement- or asphalt-stabilized drainage layers, matching the porosity of the drainage layer to the anticipated needs for quick evacuation of water; the design balances the need for stability against the need for porosity, with stability taking precedence. Drainage layers can increase restraint forces, resulting in early cracking. Unstabilized open-graded aggregate drainage layers are not recommended for pavements used by wide-body aircraft, since these layers do not provide the necessary stability and construction-related problems (rutting due to construction traffic) are common; if an unstabilized open-graded layer is necessary, it should be placed deeper in the pavement structure to reduce stresses on the layer. Drainage layer thickness is typically 100 to 150 mm (4 to 6 in.), with no individual layer less than 75 mm (3 in.) in thickness.
key_points: Rigid pavement designs include a drainage layer by default unless the subgrade is highly permeable; concrete is normally placed directly on it.
Drainage layer options: open-graded unstabilized/stabilized with subgrade or asphalt cement, open-graded with a choke stone surface, or a rapid-draining sand-fraction material.
Design balances stability against porosity, with stability taking precedence; drainage layers can increase restraint forces and early cracking.
Unstabilized open-graded drainage layers are not recommended under wide-body aircraft pavements due to stability and rutting concerns; if used, place deeper in the structure.
Common practice: cement- or asphalt-stabilized drainage layers matched in porosity to anticipated water-evacuation needs.
Typical drainage layer thickness: 100 to 150 mm (4 to 6 in.); no individual layer less than 75 mm (3 in.).
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the material type, porosity, and thickness of a drainage layer beneath a rigid concrete pavement section.

sections.title: Construction Issues
sections.summary: Explains that stabilized bases, while providing a rigid, uniform paving platform, also increase slab warping/curling and frictional restraint, shortening the joint-sawing window and raising random-cracking risk, and describes mitigation via curing membrane/geotextile applications and adjusted joint spacing/saw-cutting timing.
sections.body: Stabilized bases provide rigid paving platforms and uniform pavement support; however, they also have the potential to increase slab warping, curling, and frictional restraint forces on the concrete slab. This shortens the window of joint sawing opportunity and increases the potential for random cracking in the pavement. The designer must consider these issues in the joint layout and construction specifications for a concrete pavement placed on a stabilized base course. For cement-stabilized materials, an application of a double coat of wax-based curing membrane or a geotextile will reduce restraint; if the surface is trimmed after curing, another coat of curing membrane should be applied. As the strength of a cement-stabilized layer increases, the joint spacing of the pavement should be reduced and joints should be saw cut as soon as possible.
key_points: Stabilized bases give rigid, uniform support but increase slab warping, curling, and frictional restraint.
Increased restraint shortens the joint-sawing window and raises the potential for random cracking.
For cement-stabilized materials, a double coat of wax-based curing membrane or a geotextile reduces restraint; reapply curing membrane if the surface is trimmed after curing.
As stabilized-layer strength increases, reduce pavement joint spacing and saw cut joints as soon as possible.
The designer must account for these restraint/cracking issues in joint layout and construction specifications.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing joint spacing, curing procedures, and construction specifications for pavement placed over a stabilized base course.

sections.title: Troubleshooting Guide
sections.summary: Introduces and enumerates Table 5-1, a Problem/Probable Cause/Corrective Action diagnostic table covering three common stabilized/granular base and subbase field problems: a loose-appearing surface, depressions or excessive roller movement, and bird baths on the finished grade.
sections.body: Table 5-1 provides a list of various stabilized base problems, the probable causes, and suggested corrective actions. For granular base and subbase where the surface appears loose, probable causes are low density, a lift too thick for compaction, or insufficient rolling; the corrective action is to check moisture content and density, then re-condition to optimum moisture and re-compact the area. For granular base and subbase showing depressions or excessive movement under the roller, probable causes are high moisture content or a weak layer under the base or subbase; the corrective action is to check moisture content and re-condition to optimum if high, and to probe the grade with a dynamic cone penetrometer (DCP) to find the weak layer and stabilize the area. For bird baths on the finished grade, the probable cause is improper grade control; the corrective action is to perform a grade survey and correct deficient areas.
key_points: Problem: granular base/subbase surface appears loose. Cause: low density, lift too thick for compaction, or insufficient rolling. Action: check moisture/density, re-condition to optimum, and re-compact.

Problem: depressions or excessive movement under roller. Cause: high moisture content or a weak layer under the base/subbase. Action: check/re-condition moisture, probe with DCP to find the weak layer, and stabilize.
Problem: bird baths on finished grade. Cause: improper grade control. Action: perform a grade survey and correct deficient areas.
Table 5-1 is a Problem / Probable Cause / Corrective Action diagnostic table for stabilized and granular base course field issues.
tables: Table 5-1: Troubleshooting Guide for Stabilized Base Courses
sections.applicability: Applies when diagnosing and correcting field problems observed on granular or stabilized base and subbase courses.
